name: Skeptical Inquiry Method
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Method, Not the Mood: One Repeatable Way to Ask Good Questions
lesson.summary: The skeptical inquiry method compresses everything this course has taught about bias, leverage points, and transferable questioning into one repeatable five step sequence you can run on any claim, in any field, in the time it takes to read a headline.
lesson.body:
Skepticism can feel, from the outside, like a personality trait, a certain wary squint some people have and others do not. Everything in this course has been trying to show something different: skepticism done well is a method, a specific, repeatable sequence of steps that produces a calibrated conclusion regardless of who is running it or how exciting the claim sounds in the moment. This chapter writes that method down as one sequence, drawing directly on how biases compound, breaking the hype loop, and applying skepticism broadly, so it can be picked up and run on the next claim you encounter, quantum or otherwise.

The sequence has five steps. First, state the claim precisely, in its narrowest, most specific, most checkable form, resisting the urge to react to the more dramatic version a headline or pitch implies. Second, name your own exposure, ask explicitly which biases this specific claim is likely to activate in you, anchoring on an early number, sunk cost from a previous decision you have already made, bandwagon pressure from others who already believe it, because how biases compound showed that these rarely arrive one at a time, and naming them in advance is most of what interrupts the loop. Third, check the base rate and ask what extraordinary evidence would be required, using the same logic that powers Sagan's rule, matching the amount of evidence you demand to how much the claim would need to overturn if true. Fourth, ask who benefits from you believing this and on what timeline, since funding rounds, budget votes, and career incentives predictably cluster around the moments claims get made. Fifth, find your actual leverage point, the specific, realistic action available to you right now, whether that is asking one more question before a vote, requesting an independent replication before funding a program, or simply declining to repeat an unverified claim, because breaking the hype loop showed that low leverage reactions get absorbed by the system while a well placed one can actually interrupt it.

Run the whole sequence on one example, start to finish. Suppose a colleague forwards you an article claiming a research group has achieved room temperature, ambient pressure quantum error correction, framed as removing the biggest obstacle to practical quantum computers. Step one: the precise claim is not "quantum computing is solved," it is a specific technical result under specific conditions, and the article's framing needs to be separated from what the underlying paper actually reports. Step two: notice the pull toward believing it, because it would be exciting news and because sharing it first carries a small social reward, both of which are optimism bias and something like FOMO operating on you personally, not on the technology. Step three: this claim, if fully true as framed, would overturn a great deal of what specialists currently believe about the coherence and cryogenics challenges covered earlier in this course, which makes it a genuinely extraordinary claim requiring independent replication, not a single lab's press release, before it earns real belief. Step four: check whether the announcement's timing lines up with a funding round or a conference keynote, which would not prove the claim false but would explain why now. Step five: your actual leverage point is small but real, you can decline to forward it further until independent replication appears, and you can ask, out loud, what the replication status is when the topic comes up, which is a genuinely higher leverage act than either believing it uncritically or dismissing it uncritically.

It is worth being explicit about what this method is not. It is not a way to win arguments by being the most doubtful person in the room, and a reader who uses it that way has missed the point as badly as a reader who never developed any skepticism at all. Applying skepticism broadly was clear that real calibration moves in both directions, genuinely extraordinary evidence should change your mind toward belief just as reliably as it protects you from overclaiming. The method's output is not always "this is hype." Sometimes, run honestly, it is "this claim is precise, the evidence offered actually meets the bar, and the base rate objection does not hold up," and recognizing that outcome is just as much a successful run of the method as catching a red flag is.

What makes this a method rather than a mood is that it produces the same structure of answer regardless of subject matter, a precisely stated claim, an accounted for set of personal biases, a base rate and evidence bar, an incentive check, and a concrete next action, whether the claim in front of you is about quantum error correction, a new medical treatment, or a political statistic in an election ad. That transferability is the entire reason this course spent so long on one technology's hype cycle in the first place, and it is the tool the final chapter puts to work on the broadest possible question this course can ask: not just how to read one claim well, but how to actually decide where to place a bet.
